units.title: Number and algebra

units.title: Functions
units.blurb: Graphs, composite and inverse functions, quadratics, rational, exponential and logarithmic functions, transformations.

units.title: Geometry and trigonometry
units.blurb: 3D solids, triangle trigonometry, radians, trig identities and graphs and, at HL, vectors, lines and planes.

units.title: Statistics and probability
units.blurb: Data summaries, regression, probability, binomial and normal distributions and, at HL, continuous random variables.

units.title: Calculus
units.blurb: Limits, differentiation, integration and kinematics and, at HL, further techniques, differential equations and series.

ia.name: Mathematical exploration

criteria.name: Presentation
look: A clear aim near the start and a short rationale for the topic
A logical structure that a classmate could follow from introduction to conclusion
Concise writing with nothing irrelevant or repeated
Graphs, tables and diagrams placed where they are discussed

criteria.name: Mathematical communication
look: Correct notation and terminology throughout, with no calculator syntax such as x^2 or *
Variables and key terms defined before they are used
Formulae, graphs, tables and diagrams chosen to suit the mathematics
Graphs with labelled axes and scales; equations numbered when referred to again

criteria.name: Personal engagement
look: Your own question, data, model or approach drives the work
Independent or creative thinking rather than a reproduced textbook derivation
Your own follow-up questions, conjectures and tests of them

criteria.name: Reflection
look: Reflection throughout, not only in a final paragraph
Discussion of what each result means, its limitations and its implications
Critical comments on assumptions, accuracy and possible extensions

criteria.name: Use of mathematics
look: Mathematics relevant to the aim and at least at the level of your course
Correct algebra, calculus and calculations, with technology output interpreted
Explaining why methods work shows thorough understanding
HL: rigour and sophistication, e.g. justified generalisations or proofs

checklist: The aim is stated in the introduction and revisited in the conclusion
Length is within 12–20 pages and nothing essential is hidden in an appendix
Every variable is defined before use
No calculator notation: write x², eˣ and ×, not x^2, e^x and *
Each graph has a title, labelled axes and scales
Key algebra and calculus steps are shown and explained, not only stated
Technology output (regressions, numerical solutions) is explained in words
Assumptions and limitations are discussed where they arise
General results are justified or proved where possible (essential at HL)
All sources, data and images are referenced consistently
A classmate could follow the argument without your help

examTips: Paper 1 has no calculator: practise exact values (sin π/6, ln e, surds) and leave answers exact unless told otherwise.
On Paper 2, give answers to 3 significant figures (angles in degrees to 1 d.p.) and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.
"Show that" means every step must be visible; you cannot work backwards from the given answer, but you may use it in later parts.
Write down the equation or integral you solve on the GDC, not just the result; method marks are lost with a bare wrong answer.
Check the mode and the domain: radians in calculus, and reject solutions outside the given interval or that make a logarithm undefined.
